Their brief term lasts until the end of August, highlighting the fluid nature of Roman political appointments.
events.name: May – Aulus Larcius Macedo, the former Governor of Galatia; and Publius Ducenius Verres take office for four months as the suffect consuls to succeed Bellicius and Glabrio, and serve until the end of August

events.enhanced_description: In September, Gaius Valerius Severus and Gaius Julius Gallus take over as consuls in Rome, replacing the previous suffect consuls. Their leadership continues until the end of the year, contributing to the ongoing political dynamics of the Roman Republic.
events.name: September – Gaius Valerius Severus and Gaius Julius Gallus replace consuls Larcius and Ducenius and serve until the end of the year

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian initiates the reconstruction of the Olympeion, a grand temple dedicated to Zeus in Athens. This project reflects Hadrian's admiration for Greek culture and his desire to leave a lasting architectural legacy in the city.
events.name: Emperor Hadrian begins to rebuild the Olympeion in Athens

events.enhanced_description: Antinous, a young Greek boy, becomes the beloved companion of Emperor Hadrian during his travels across the Roman Empire. Their close relationship is celebrated in art and literature, symbolizing Hadrian's personal affections and the cultural exchanges of the time.
events.name: Antinous becomes Hadrian's beloved companion on his journeys through the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: During his voyage to Greece, Emperor Hadrian participates in the Eleusinian Mysteries, ancient rites held in Eleusis that celebrate the myth of Demeter and Persephone. This initiation reflects Hadrian's deep engagement with Greek religious traditions and his desire to connect with the cultural heritage of the region.
events.name: During a voyage to Greece, Hadrian is initiated in the ancient rites known as the Eleusinian Mysteries

events.enhanced_description: Nahapana, the ruler of the Scythians, is defeated in battle by King Gautamiputra Satakarni of the Satavahana dynasty in northern India. This significant victory leads to the collapse of the Scythian dynasty in the region and solidifies Satakarni's power.
events.name: In northern India, Nahapana, ruler of the Scythians, is defeated and dies in battle while fighting against King Gautamiputra Satakarni

events.enhanced_description: Fregellae's revolt against Roman rule began as a response to the oppressive policies of the Roman Republic. The revolt was ultimately crushed, leading to the destruction of the city and a significant loss of life, marking a pivotal moment in the struggle between Rome and its Italian allies.
events.name: Fregellae's Revolt Against Rome

events.enhanced_description: Mithridates II ascended to the throne of Parthia following the reign of Artabanus II, marking a significant period of expansion and consolidation for the Parthian Empire. His reign is noted for its military successes and diplomatic relations with neighboring powers.
events.name: Mithridates II Succeeds Artabanus II as King of Parthia

events.enhanced_description: The reconciliation between Cleopatra II and her brother Ptolemy VIII was a crucial moment in the Ptolemaic dynasty, which had been marked by internal strife and power struggles. This event helped stabilize their rule over Egypt during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Cleopatra II and Ptolemy VIII Reconcile

events.enhanced_description: Li Xi and Zhang Cigong led an invasion into Xiongnu territory from Youbeiping Prefecture, but encountered no resistance from enemy forces. This lack of opposition indicated a potential shift in the Xiongnu's military strategy or readiness.
events.name: Li Xi and Zhang Cigong's Invasion of Xiongnu Territory

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Wu of Han recognized the military achievements of General Wei Qing by appointing him as General-in-Chief, a significant promotion that underscored the importance of military leadership in the Han Dynasty's expansionist policies.
events.name: Emperor Wu Rewards Wei Qing

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic military campaign, Han general Wei Qing led a cavalry force into Xiongnu territory, successfully surrounding the Tuqi King of the Right during a night attack. This operation showcased the Han Dynasty's military prowess and its ongoing conflict with the Xiongnu tribes.
events.name: Wei Qing's Campaign Against the Xiongnu

events.enhanced_description: In a retaliatory move, the Xiongnu invaded the Prefecture of Dai, resulting in the death of its chief commandant, Zhu Ying. This attack highlighted the ongoing conflict between the Han Dynasty and the nomadic Xiongnu tribes.
events.name: Xiongnu Retaliation Against Dai Prefecture

events.enhanced_description: The Pantheon, one of the most iconic buildings of ancient Rome, is constructed under the reign of Emperor Hadrian. This architectural marvel, known for its massive dome and oculus, serves as a temple for all gods and exemplifies the grandeur of Roman engineering and design.
events.name: The Pantheon is constructed (in Rome) as it stands today, by Hadrian

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian establishes the Panhellenion, a league of Greek cities aimed at promoting unity and cultural exchange among the Hellenistic world. This initiative reflects Hadrian's admiration for Greek culture and his efforts to strengthen ties across the empire.
events.name: Emperor Hadrian establishes the Panhellenion

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian implements a land distribution policy, allocating imperial lands to small farmers in an effort to bolster the agrarian economy and support rural communities. This reform is part of Hadrian's broader agenda to improve the welfare of the Roman populace.
events.name: Hadrian distributes imperial lands to small farmers

events.enhanced_description: Construction of Hadrian's Villa in Tivoli, Italy, begins, showcasing the emperor's passion for architecture and the arts. This expansive estate becomes a retreat for Hadrian, reflecting his travels and the diverse influences he encountered throughout the empire.

events.name: Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli, Italy, starts to be built (approximate date)

events.enhanced_description: A devastating plague sweeps through North Africa, exacerbated by a locust invasion that has ravaged cropland. The resulting famine leads to significant loss of life, with estimates of up to 500,000 deaths in Numidia alone, highlighting the vulnerability of agrarian societies to environmental disasters.
events.name: Plague sweeps North Africa in the wake of a locust invasion that destroys large areas of cropland

events.enhanced_description: The last year of the Yanguang era marks a significant period in the Han dynasty, characterized by political instability and the eventual transition to the Yongjian era. This era was marked by the reign of Emperor An, who faced challenges from court factions and the growing influence of eunuchs.
events.name: Last (4th) year of the Yanguang era of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 125 AD, the Han dynasty witnessed a significant transition of power as Emperor Han Andi was succeeded by the Marquis of Beixiang, followed by Han Shundi. This change was indicative of the shifting political landscape within the court, influenced by powerful eunuchs and noble families.
events.name: Change of emperor of the Chinese Han dynasty from Han Andi to Marquis of Beixiang, then to Han Shundi

events.enhanced_description: Gautamiputra Satakarni, a prominent king of the Andhra dynasty, successfully conquered the Konkan region, extending his influence across central India. This military achievement solidified his power and control over trade routes along the western coast.
events.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni conquers the Konkan near Bombay

events.enhanced_description: Zhang Heng, a renowned polymath of the Han dynasty, invented a hydraulic-powered armillary sphere, which was a significant advancement in astronomical instruments. This invention allowed for more accurate observations of celestial bodies and contributed to the development of Chinese astronomy.
events.name: Zhang Heng invents a hydraulic-powered armillary sphere

events.enhanced_description: The epoch of the Javanese calendar marks the beginning of a significant cultural and temporal framework for the Javanese people. This calendar system has influenced agricultural practices, religious observances, and social organization in Java.
events.name: The epoch of the Javanese calendar begins

events.enhanced_description: In his Satires, the Roman poet Juvenal famously critiques the political apathy of the populace, suggesting that the provision of bread and circuses is sufficient to keep the citizens content. This phrase has since become emblematic of the use of superficial appeasement in politics.
events.name: The Satires of Juvenal intimate that bread and circuses keep the Roman people happy

events.enhanced_description: Pope Telesphorus, recognized as the eighth pope in Roman Catholic tradition, succeeded Pope Sixtus I during a time of early Christian consolidation and growth. His papacy is noted for its emphasis on the celebration of Easter and the establishment of certain liturgical practices.
events.name: Pope Telesphorus succeeds Pope Sixtus I

events.enhanced_description: Cleopatra Thea ascended to power in the Seleucid Empire following the death of Seleucus V, appointing Antiochus VIII Grypus as co-ruler. Her reign was marked by political maneuvering and attempts to stabilize the empire amidst external threats.
events.name: Cleopatra Thea Succeeds Seleucus V

events.enhanced_description: In Rome, Marcus Fulvius Flaccus proposed extending Roman citizenship to northern Italians, a move that was met with resistance from the Senate, leading to his reassignment to quell disturbances in Massilia. This event marked the beginning of a broader campaign for citizenship rights in the Republic.
events.name: Marcus Fulvius Flaccus Proposes Citizenship Extension

events.enhanced_description: The completion of the Aqua Tepula aqueduct in Rome represented a significant advancement in engineering and urban infrastructure, enhancing the city's water supply and public health. This project was part of a broader trend of aqueduct construction during the Roman Republic.
events.name: Completion of Aqua Tepula Aqueduct

events.enhanced_description: In retaliation for the Han conquest of the Ordos Plateau, Xiongnu forces launched raids on the Prefectures of Dai, Dingxiang, and Shang, demonstrating the ongoing hostilities between the Han Dynasty and the nomadic tribes. These raids were part of a larger cycle of conflict in the region.
events.name: Xiongnu Raids in Retaliation for Han Conquest

events.enhanced_description: The Xiongnu Tuqi of the Right launched an invasion in response to the loss of the Ordos Plateau, resulting in significant casualties among officials and civilians. This invasion underscored the volatility of the region and the Xiongnu's aggressive stance against Han encroachments.
events.name: Xiongnu Invasion Led by Tuqi

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian ordered the demolition of the old Pantheon in Rome to make way for a new structure that would become one of the most iconic buildings of ancient Rome. The new Pantheon, completed later, is celebrated for its architectural innovation and grandeur.
events.name: Demolition of the old Pantheon by Emperor Hadrian

events.enhanced_description: The first year of the Yongjian era marks the beginning of a new reign under Emperor Shun of Han, following the tumultuous period of the previous era. This era is characterized by attempts to stabilize the Han dynasty amidst internal strife and external pressures.
events.name: First year of the Yongjian era of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The successful revolt of Tyre from the Seleucid Empire marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, reflecting the growing discontent among the cities under Seleucid control. This event was part of the broader struggle for autonomy in the face of imperial rule.
events.name: Tyre Revolts from the Seleucid Empire

events.enhanced_description: Seleucus V Philometor succeeded his father Demetrius II as king of the Seleucid Empire, with his stepmother Cleopatra Thea acting as regent due to his youth. This transition of power was critical in maintaining stability within the empire during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Seleucus V Philometor Succeeds Demetrius II

events.enhanced_description: The death of Junchen Chanyu marked a pivotal moment in Xiongnu leadership, as his brother Yizhixie seized power by overthrowing Junchen's son. This power shift had significant implications for the Xiongnu's relations with neighboring states, particularly the Han Dynasty.
events.name: Death of Junchen Chanyu and Succession of Yizhixie

events.enhanced_description: After escaping imprisonment during the Xiongnu civil war, the diplomat Zhang Qian returned to China, bringing valuable reports about the lands to the west. His journeys significantly contributed to the Han dynasty's understanding of Central Asia and laid the groundwork for future diplomatic and trade relations along the Silk Road.
events.name: Zhang Qian's Return to China

events.enhanced_description: In retaliation for the Han conquest of the Ordos Plateau, the Xiongnu launched a brutal invasion of the province of Dai, resulting in the death of its governor, Gong You, and the capture of over 1000 inhabitants. This event marked a significant escalation in the conflict between the Han dynasty and the Xiongnu, illustrating the volatility of the region during this period.
events.name: Xiongnu Invasion of Dai

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 126 BC, the Xiongnu crossed into Yanmen, where they killed or captured over 1000 inhabitants. This attack was part of a broader campaign against Han territories, demonstrating the ongoing threat posed by the Xiongnu to the Han dynasty.
events.name: Xiongnu Attack on Yanmen

events.enhanced_description: After a seven-year journey through the provinces, Emperor Hadrian returned to Rome, bringing with him insights and experiences that would influence his policies and architectural projects. His travels were pivotal in shaping the Roman Empire's administration and military strategy.
events.name: Emperor Hadrian returns to Rome

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian, advised by his proconsul Gaius Minicius Fundanus, established a policy that Christians should not be executed without a trial. This marked a significant moment in the relationship between the Roman state and early Christianity, reflecting a shift towards more formal legal proceedings.
events.name: Hadrian's decree on Christian trials

events.enhanced_description: Kanishka I ascended to the throne of the Kushan Empire, a significant power in Central Asia, known for its cultural and economic prosperity. His reign is often associated with the spread of Buddhism and the flourishing of trade along the Silk Road.
events.name: Kanishka I starts to rule in the Kushan Empire

events.enhanced_description: The philosopher Carpocrates articulated a radical view that rejected the concept of private property, arguing that it was contrary to Christian teachings. His ideas contributed to early Christian debates about materialism and communal living.
events.name: Carpocrates rejects ownership of private property

events.enhanced_description: In 127 BC, the Scythians achieved a significant victory over the Parthians in a battle around Media. This defeat showcased the shifting power dynamics in the region and the ongoing conflicts between nomadic tribes and established kingdoms.
events.name: Scythians Defeat Parthians

events.enhanced_description: In January 127 BC, Emperor Wu of Han initiated a policy that allowed client kings to divide their kingdoms, enabling younger brothers and sons to inherit land. This reform aimed to strengthen imperial control and prevent the consolidation of power among local rulers, thereby enhancing the stability of the Han dynasty.
events.name: Emperor Wu's Land Division Policy

events.enhanced_description: In 127 BC, Han general Wei Qing achieved a decisive victory against a Xiongnu army near Gaoque, subsequently invading the Ordos Plateau. His military campaigns were pivotal in reasserting Han dominance over northern territories and led to the establishment of the Shuofang Commandery.
events.name: Wei Qing's Victory Against Xiongnu

events.enhanced_description: In 127 BC, the Han dynasty rationalized its northern frontier by abandoning the remote region of Zaoyang to the Xiongnu. This strategic withdrawal reflected the challenges faced by the Han in maintaining control over distant territories amidst ongoing conflicts with nomadic tribes.
events.name: Han Abandonment of Zaoyang

events.enhanced_description: During his inspection of the Roman province of North Africa, Emperor Hadrian visited Lambaesis to oversee Legio III Augusta. This legion was strategically positioned in the Aurès Mountains to maintain order and defend against potential threats.
events.name: Hadrian inspects Legio III Augusta in North Africa

events.enhanced_description: Hadrian's Wall was completed under the orders of Emperor Hadrian, serving as a defensive fortification marking the northern limit of the Roman Empire in Britain. The wall included numerous forts and watch towers, showcasing Roman engineering prowess.
events.name: Completion of Hadrian's Wall

events.enhanced_description: The decline of agriculture in the Roman Empire was exacerbated by the influx of grain imports from Egypt and North Africa, which depressed local wheat prices. This economic shift forced many farmers into poverty and off their lands, leading to social unrest.
events.name: Decline of Roman agriculture

events.enhanced_description: In Rome, bakeries flourished, producing a wide variety of bread types, which became a staple of the Roman diet. The distribution of free bread to the poor was a key aspect of Roman social policy, aimed at maintaining public order.
events.name: Roman bakeries produce dozens of bread varieties

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian commenced a comprehensive inspection of the provinces of Greece, Asia Minor, and Egypt, aiming to assess and improve the administration and military readiness of these vital regions of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Hadrian begins inspection of provinces

events.enhanced_description: King Gaeru ascended to the throne of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, marking the beginning of a significant period in the kingdom's history. His reign is noted for cultural development and military engagements with neighboring states.
events.name: King Gaeru of Baekje succeeds to the throne

events.enhanced_description: In Dalmatia, the discovery of fossils from large prehistoric animals marked an important moment in the study of paleontology. These findings contributed to the understanding of the region's ancient ecosystems and biodiversity.
events.name: Discovery of prehistoric animal fossils in Dalmatia

events.enhanced_description: The Pantheon, one of the most remarkable architectural achievements of ancient Rome, was completed during this period. Its innovative design and massive dome have made it a lasting symbol of Roman engineering and architecture.
events.name: Completion of the Pantheon in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 128 BC, the Tokhari overran the Greco-Bactrian kingdom, marking a significant shift in power in Central Asia. This event contributed to the decline of Hellenistic influence in the region and the rise of new powers.
events.name: Tokhari Overrun of Greco-Bactrian Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: Around 128 BC, Artabanus II ascended to the throne of Parthia, a period marked by political intrigue and conflict within the Parthian Empire. His reign would influence the dynamics of power in the region, particularly in relation to Rome and the neighboring kingdoms.
events.name: Artabanus II Becomes King of Parthia

events.enhanced_description: In 128 or 127 BC, the Xiongnu launched a significant invasion of northern China, resulting in the death of the governor of Liaoxi and the defeat of Han general Han Anguo. This incursion exemplified the ongoing hostilities between the Xiongnu and the Han dynasty, with the Xiongnu capturing thousands of inhabitants from the affected regions.
events.name: Xiongnu Invasion of Northern China

events.enhanced_description: In 128 BC, Han general Wei Qing, commanding an army of 30,000 cavalrymen, defeated a Xiongnu army north of Yanmen. This victory was part of a broader campaign against the Xiongnu, showcasing the military prowess of the Han forces during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Wei Qing's Victory North of Yanmen

events.enhanced_description: After spending a year in Greater Yuezhi, the Han diplomat Zhang Qian began his return journey to China in 128 BC. Despite failing to secure an alliance against the Xiongnu, his travels provided invaluable insights into the cultures and geography of Central Asia.
events.name: Zhang Qian's Return Journey

events.enhanced_description: In 128 BC, Limenius composed the Second Delphic Hymn, a significant work in ancient Greek music. This composition reflects the cultural and artistic developments of the time, particularly in relation to religious practices at the Oracle of Delphi.
events.name: Composition of the Second Delphic Hymn

events.enhanced_description: Legio III Augusta constructed a defensive fortification in Lambaesis, Algeria, to secure the region of Numidia. This military installation was crucial for maintaining Roman control and protecting against local uprisings.
events.name: Construction of a defense for Numidia at Lambaesis

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Hadrian continued his extensive inspections of the provinces, focusing on Caria, Cappadocia, and Syria. These visits were part of his broader strategy to enhance governance and military readiness across the empire.
events.name: Hadrian inspects Caria, Cappadocia, and Syria

events.enhanced_description: The song 'Angel's Hymn' was composed, reflecting the rich cultural and artistic expressions of the time. This piece is emblematic of the evolving musical traditions within the Roman Empire.
events.name: Creation of the song 'Angel's Hymn'

events.enhanced_description: In 130 AD, a significant legal reform was enacted in Rome, prohibiting the execution of slaves without a trial. This law marked a progressive step in the treatment of slaves within the Roman legal system, reflecting a shift towards more humane practices.
events.name: A law is passed in Rome banning the execution of slaves without a trial

events.enhanced_description: The Temple of Olympian Zeus, a monumental structure in Athens, was completed in 130 AD, showcasing the grandeur of Hellenistic architecture. Designed by the architect Cossutius, this temple was dedicated to Zeus, the king of the Greek gods, and served as a symbol of Athenian power and religious devotion.
events.name: The Temple of Olympian Zeus is completed at Athens

events.enhanced_description: In 130 AD, Emperor Hadrian undertook a notable visit to the cities of Petra and Gerasa, enhancing Roman influence in the region. His visit was part of a broader effort to integrate and Romanize the provinces, showcasing the empire's architectural and cultural achievements.
events.name: Emperor Hadrian visits the cities Petra and Gerasa (Jerash)

events.enhanced_description: The construction of a Triumphal Arch in Gerasa (modern-day Jerash) in 130 AD commemorated Emperor Hadrian's visit and celebrated the prosperity of the city. This architectural marvel exemplified Roman engineering and served as a symbol of the emperor's favor.
events.name: A Triumphal Arch for Hadrian is built in Gerasa

events.enhanced_description: In 130 AD, construction began on Canopus, a significant feature of Hadrian's Villa in Tivoli. This architectural project reflected Hadrian's admiration for Greek culture and his desire to create a luxurious retreat that blended various cultural influences.
events.name: Construction begins on Canopus, Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli, Italy

events.enhanced_description: In 130 AD, Huviska ascended to the throne of the Kushan Empire, a significant power in North India. His reign is noted for the promotion of trade, culture, and the arts, as well as the spread of Buddhism throughout the region.
events.name: Huviska becomes king of the Kushan Empire in India

events.enhanced_description: Around 130 AD, Rudradaman I, the Scythian king, successfully reconquered territories previously annexed by Gautamiputra from the Andhra dynasty. This military campaign was pivotal in re-establishing Scythian dominance in the region.
events.name: The Scythian king Rudradaman I reconquers the lands annexed by Gautamiputra from the Andhra

events.enhanced_description: In 130 AD, the renowned Greek scholar Claudius Ptolemaeus made significant contributions to optics by tabulating angles of refraction for various media. His work laid the groundwork for future studies in optics and influenced later scientists.

image.caption: Pages from Ptolemy’s *Almagest*, with Arabic text and astronomical tables.
image.credit: Ptolemy — The Bodleian Library, University of Oxford
image.date_qualification: The manuscript is dated 1397, long after the event dated 130 AD; this is a later work-related illustration, not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Monastery of St. Macarius, Wadi El Natrun

events.name: Claudius Ptolemaeus tabulates angles of refraction for several media

events.enhanced_description: The Antinous Mondragone, a celebrated sculpture depicting Antinous, was created around 130 AD. This artwork exemplifies the artistic style of the period and reflects the cultural significance of Antinous, a favorite of Emperor Hadrian.

image.caption: Marble portrait bust of Antinous, known as the Antinous Mondragone.
image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist — Marie-Lan Nguyen (2011)
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the Antinous Mondragone, a sculpture made circa 130–138 AD; image date is circa 130 AD.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Antinous Mondragone is sculpted

events.enhanced_description: Between 130 and 138 AD, sculptural reliefs depicting Hadrian hunting boar and sacrificing to Apollo were crafted for the Arch of Constantine in Rome. These reliefs highlight the artistic achievements of the era and the emperor's connection to divine favor.

image.caption: South side of the Arch of Constantine, viewed from Via Triumphalis.
image.date_qualification: A 2022 photograph of the arch, not a depiction of the Hadrianic reliefs being made.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Hadrian Hunting Boar and Sacrificing to Apollo, sculptural reliefs on the Arch of Constantine, Rome, are made

events.enhanced_description: Around 130 to 138 AD, the statue of Antinous was sculpted at Hadrian's Villa in Tivoli. This statue is a prime example of Roman portraiture and reflects the deep admiration Hadrian had for Antinous, who was his beloved companion.
events.name: Antinous, from Hadrian's Villa at Tivoli, Italy, is made

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, Emperor Hadrian established the city of Aelia Capitolina on the site of Jerusalem, following the destruction of the Second Temple. This act was part of Hadrian's broader strategy to Romanize the region and erase Jewish identity.

image.caption: Roman coin of Aelia Capitolina depicting Hadrian as priest-founder plowing with a team of oxen.
image.date_qualification: The depicted coin was struck in 136 CE; the image file’s stated original date is 2005.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Emperor Hadrian builds the city Aelia Capitolina, on the location of Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, under the orders of Emperor Hadrian, Salvius Julianus codified the Praetor's Edict, which standardized legal practices in Rome. This codification marked a significant development in Roman law, ensuring greater consistency and clarity in legal proceedings.
events.name: The Praetor's Edict is definitively codified by Salvius Julianus, on Hadrian's orders

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, Emperor Hadrian implemented a reorganization of the Imperial Council, reinforcing central administration and assigning administrative roles to knights. This restructuring diminished the Senate's power, reflecting Hadrian's vision for a more centralized governance.
events.name: Reorganization of the Imperial Council: Central administration is reinforced

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, Emperor Hadrian reinstated the monarchist policies of his predecessors, Claudius and Domitian. This restoration granted the equestrian order greater legal status, reshaping the political landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Hadrian restores the monarchist policy of Claudius and Domitian

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, Italy was reorganized into legal districts overseen by consuls, a move that significantly reduced the Senate's influence and authority. This administrative change was part of Hadrian's broader strategy to centralize power within the imperial government.
events.name: Italy is divided into legal districts managed by consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, the Edict of Hadrian was issued, prohibiting the practice of circumcision among Jews. This decree, along with restrictions on the public reading of the Torah and other religious practices, intensified tensions between the Roman authorities and the Jewish population.
events.name: The Edict of Hadrian prohibits the practice of circumcision

events.enhanced_description: In 131 AD, the Temple of Baalshamin was constructed in Palmyra, reflecting the city's importance as a cultural and religious center in the Roman Empire. This temple was dedicated to the god Baalshamin, showcasing the blend of Roman and local traditions.

image.caption: Temple of Baalshamin in Palmyra, Syria.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2010-04-07; the image documents the later site, not the 131 AD rebuilding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Temple of Baalshamin is built in Palmyra

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens was completed, designed by the architect Cossutius. This monumental temple, dedicated to the chief deity of the Greek pantheon, exemplified the grandeur of Hellenistic architecture and served as a testament to Athenian cultural pride.
events.name: The Temple of Olympian Zeus (Athens) is completed, using Cossutius' design

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, the Bar Kokhba revolt began as Simon bar Kokhba led a Jewish uprising against Roman rule in Judea, seeking to establish an independent state. Supported by Rabbi Akiva, the revolt initially gained traction but was ultimately crushed by Emperor Hadrian's forces in 135 AD.
events.name: Bar Kokhba revolt

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, the Roman Legion X Fretensis was forced to evacuate Jerusalem and retreat to Caesarea due to the escalating conflict during the Bar Kokhba revolt. This retreat allowed Jewish forces to temporarily re-establish their sacrificial system in the city.
events.name: Legio X Fretensis must evacuate Jerusalem, returning to Caesarea

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, merchants began constructing structures outside the forts of Hadrian's Wall in Britain, providing goods and services to Roman soldiers. This development highlighted the economic interactions between the military and local populations in a region with limited currency.
events.name: Merchants in Britain build structures outside the forts of Hadrian's Wall

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, construction commenced on the Mausoleum of Hadrian, known today as Castel Sant'Angelo, in Rome. This monumental tomb was designed as a final resting place for Emperor Hadrian and later became a significant symbol of imperial power.
events.name: Construction begins on the Mausoleum of Hadrian in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, the era name of the Han dynasty transitioned from Yongjian to Yangjia, marking a new phase in the imperial calendar. This change reflects the administrative practices of the Han dynasty and its emphasis on continuity and legitimacy.
events.name: Change of era name from Yongjian to Yangjia of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 132 AD, the Chinese polymath Zhang Heng invented the first seismometer, a groundbreaking device that could detect and determine the direction of earthquakes. This invention demonstrated advanced understanding of seismic activity and laid the foundation for future geological studies.
events.name: Chinese scientist Zhang Heng invents the first seismometer

events.enhanced_description: The Bar Kokhba Revolt was a major Jewish uprising against Roman rule in Judea, led by Simon bar Kokhba. In response to the revolt, the Roman governor Sextus Julius Severus was dispatched to restore order, ultimately leading to a brutal campaign that resulted in significant loss of life and the establishment of a Roman military presence in the region.
events.name: Bar Kokhba Revolt: Sextus Julius Severus sent to Judea

events.enhanced_description: In 134 AD, a significant law was enacted in Rome aimed at improving the conditions of free workers, reflecting the social and economic challenges of the time. This legislation was part of broader reforms during the Roman Empire to address labor issues and enhance the rights of workers.
events.name: Law improving conditions for free workers passed in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 134 AD, Arrianus, the Roman governor of Cappadocia, successfully repelled an attack from the Alani, a nomadic tribe from southeastern Russia. This event underscored the ongoing conflicts between the Roman Empire and various nomadic groups during this period.
events.name: Arrianus repulses Alani attack

events.enhanced_description: In 134 AD, following the suppression of the Bar Kokhba Revolt, Roman forces retook Jerusalem, which had been largely destroyed during the conflict. The city was subsequently renamed Aelia Capitolina, marking a significant shift in its governance and cultural identity under Roman rule.
events.name: Romans retake Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In 134 AD, Ilseong ascended to the throne of the Korean kingdom of Silla, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His reign marked a continuation of Silla's development as a significant cultural and political entity in East Asia.

image.caption: Korean crown and belt from the Silla era.
image.credit: David Trowbridge — originally posted to Flickr as Silla-era crown and belt
image.date_qualification: The objects are described as Silla-era; the supplied 2009 date is the photograph’s capture date, not the objects’ date or the accession date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Ilseong becomes ruler of Silla

events.enhanced_description: Hadrian's Villa, a grand architectural complex built by Emperor Hadrian, was completed in 134 AD in Tivoli, Italy. This villa served as a retreat for the emperor and is renowned for its innovative design and extensive gardens, reflecting the cultural aspirations of the Roman elite.
events.name: Completion of Hadrian's Villa

events.enhanced_description: Caius Fulvius Flaccus, serving as consul of Rome, was tasked with quelling a significant slave uprising. His military efforts culminated in the defeat of approximately 4,000 slaves at Sinuessa, a pivotal moment in the broader context of slave revolts in the Roman Republic.
events.name: Caius Fulvius Flaccus, as consul, is sent against the slaves

events.enhanced_description: Following the assassination of his father, Simon Maccabaeus, John Hyrcanus ascended to the position of high priest and prince of Judea. His leadership marked a significant period in Jewish history, characterized by territorial expansion and the consolidation of power within the Hasmonean dynasty.
events.name: John Hyrcanus becomes high priest and prince of Judea

events.enhanced_description: Under the guidance of philosopher Dong Zhongshu, Emperor Wu of Han established Confucianism as the official state philosophy, significantly influencing Chinese governance and culture. This decision underscored the importance of Confucian texts, including the Book of Rites and the I Ching, in shaping the moral framework of the Han dynasty.
events.name: Emperor Wu promotes Confucianism as the official doctrine of the Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Hipparchus, a prominent Greek astronomer, made groundbreaking contributions to the understanding of celestial mechanics by discovering the precession of the equinoxes. This discovery laid the foundation for future astronomical studies and was pivotal in the development of the field.
events.name: Hipparchus discovers the precession of the equinoxes

events.enhanced_description: Hipparchus compiled one of the earliest known star catalogues, systematically listing stars and their positions. This catalogue was instrumental for later astronomers and marked a significant advancement in the field of astronomy.
events.name: Hipparchus creates a star catalogue

events.enhanced_description: During the summer of 134 AD, Roman governor Sextus Julius Severus initiated a military campaign against the Jewish rebel strongholds in the Judean mountains. This campaign was part of the larger efforts to suppress the Bar Kokhba Revolt and reassert Roman control over the region.
events.name: Sextus Julius Severus begins campaign against Jewish rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, following the suppression of the Bar Kokhba Revolt, Emperor Hadrian barred Jews from Jerusalem, initiating a significant Jewish diaspora. This policy led to the dispersal of Jewish communities across the Roman Empire, profoundly impacting Jewish history and identity.
events.name: Jewish diaspora begins under Hadrian

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, Jerusalem was officially renamed Colonia Aelia Capitolina in honor of Emperor Hadrian. This renaming was part of Hadrian's broader efforts to Romanize the region following the Bar Kokhba Revolt, including the construction of a Roman temple at the site of the former Jewish Temple.
events.name: Jerusalem renamed Colonia Aelia Capitolina

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, an altar to Jupiter was erected on the site of the former Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, symbolizing the Roman Empire's dominance and the suppression of Jewish religious practices. This act was part of Hadrian's efforts to establish Roman religious customs in the newly renamed Colonia Aelia Capitolina.
events.name: Altar to Jupiter erected in Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, the Canopus, a significant architectural feature of Hadrian's Villa, was completed. This structure was inspired by the famous Canopus in Egypt and served as a picturesque setting for gatherings and cultural activities, reflecting Hadrian's fascination with diverse cultures.
events.name: Completion of Canopus at Hadrian's Villa

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, the Alans posed a threat to the Roman province of Cappadocia, but were repulsed by the Roman governor Arrianus. This event highlighted the ongoing military challenges faced by the Roman Empire from nomadic tribes during this period.
events.name: Alans threaten Cappadocia

events.enhanced_description: The year 135 AD marked the last year of the Yangjia era of the Han Dynasty in China. This period was characterized by significant political and social changes that would eventually lead to the decline of the Han Dynasty.
events.name: Last year of Yangjia era of Han Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 135 AD, Marcus (or Mahalia) was appointed as the bishop of Jerusalem, a position he would hold until his death in 156 AD. His leadership during a tumultuous period for the Christian community in Jerusalem was significant for the development of early Christianity.
events.name: Marcus becomes bishop of Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: The First Servile War began in Sicily, marking a significant uprising of enslaved people against their Roman masters. This conflict highlighted the tensions and struggles inherent in the Roman slave system during this period.
events.name: The First Servile War starts in Sicily

events.enhanced_description: Servius Fulvius Flaccus led Roman forces to victory against the Ardiaei, a tribal group in Illyria, effectively quelling their uprising. This military success contributed to the Roman expansion into the Balkans.
events.name: Servius Fulvius Flaccus defeats an uprising of the Ardiaei in Illyria

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Cosconius achieved a notable military victory against the Scordisci, a Celtic tribe, in Thrace. This battle was part of the broader Roman efforts to secure their influence in the region.
events.name: Marcus Cosconius defeats the Scordisci in Thrace

events.enhanced_description: The death of Menander I, a prominent king of the Indo-Greek Kingdom, marked a significant transition in the region's leadership. His successor, Epander, inherited a kingdom known for its cultural syncretism and Hellenistic influence.
events.name: Menander I, king of the Indo-Greek Kingdom dies and is succeeded by Epander

events.enhanced_description: The death of Grand Empress Dowager Dou allowed her grandson, Emperor Wu, to consolidate power and exert greater control over the Han dynasty. This shift significantly impacted the political landscape of China during this period.
events.name: Grand Empress Dowager Dou dies

events.enhanced_description: The conflict between the vassal states of Minyue and Nanyue escalated as Minyue launched an attack. The Han dynasty intervened militarily, leading to significant political changes in the region.
events.name: Minyue attacks Nanyue

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move, Emperor Wu appointed Zou Chou as the king of Minyue, solidifying Han influence in the region. This decision was part of the broader Han efforts to manage and control their vassal states.
events.name: Emperor Wu makes Zou Chou the king of Minyue

events.enhanced_description: The Han dynasty launched a military campaign against the Dian Kingdom, resulting in the establishment of a military commandery in the Yunnan region. This campaign was part of the Han's efforts to expand their territory and influence.
events.name: A Han military campaign against the Dian Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, the Roman Empire initiated a military campaign against the Suebi, a group of Germanic tribes. This conflict was part of the broader Roman efforts to secure its borders and maintain control over its provinces.
events.name: War against the Suebi begins

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, Emperor Hadrian pursued Jewish rebels from Galilee, further consolidating Roman control over the region following the Bar Kokhba Revolt. This military action was part of Hadrian's broader strategy to suppress Jewish resistance and solidify Roman authority.
events.name: Hadrian chases Jews from Galilee

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, the Roman province of Iudaea, which included Galilee, was officially renamed Syria Palaestina by Emperor Hadrian. This renaming was part of Hadrian's efforts to erase Jewish identity in the region following the Bar Kokhba Revolt.

image.caption: Bronze statue of Hadrian, discovered at a Roman army camp.
image.credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany — Bronze statue of Hadrian, found at the Camp of the Sixth Roman Legion in Tel Shalem, 117–138 AD, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
image.date_qualification: The image date is the photograph date; the statue is dated 117–138 AD in the credit.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Roman province of Iudaea becomes Syria Palaestina

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, Emperor Hadrian dictated his memoirs at his villa near Tivoli, reflecting on his reign and experiences. This act was significant as it provided insights into the thoughts and policies of one of Rome's most notable emperors.
events.name: Hadrian dictates memoirs at his villa

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, Emperor Hadrian uncovered a conspiracy involving certain senators, which highlighted the political tensions of his reign. Following this discovery, he adopted Lucius Aelius as his heir, indicating a shift in his succession plans.
events.name: Hadrian uncovers conspiracy among senators

events.enhanced_description: The year 136 AD marked the first year of the Yonghe era of the Han Dynasty in China. This era was characterized by significant political developments and cultural achievements that would influence Chinese history for centuries.
events.name: First year of Yonghe era of Han Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, Pope Hyginus succeeded Pope Telesphorus as the ninth pope of Rome, according to tradition. His papacy occurred during a time of growth and consolidation for the early Christian church amidst Roman political challenges.
events.name: Pope Hyginus succeeds Pope Telesphorus

events.enhanced_description: In 136 AD, a significant change occurred in the leadership of the Christian community in Byzantium, with Bishop Eleutherius being succeeded by Bishop Felix. This transition reflected the evolving structure of early Christian leadership in the region.
events.name: Change of Bishop of Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Wu of Han officially adopted Confucianism as the state religion, significantly shaping the philosophical and ethical landscape of China. This decision laid the groundwork for Confucian thought to permeate Chinese governance and society for centuries.

image.caption: Western Han tomb fresco depicting Confucius, found in Dongping County, Shandong Province.
image.credit: Anonymous Chinese painter of the Western Han period — Du Guodong (17 October 2007). " Frescos found in a tomb in Shandong Province ." Xinhua News, citing the Shanghai Daily. Accessed 10 October 2016. For further information, see China.org.cn (17 October 2007). " 2,000-year-old tomb frescos discovered ." Accessed 10 October 2016.
image.date_qualification: The fresco is identified as dating to the Western Han period; a photograph of it was taken on 2007-10-13. Neither date is the date of the depicted state adoption.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Confucianism is adopted as the state religion in China by Emperor Wu

events.enhanced_description: Carneades, a prominent philosopher, retired from his position as the head of the Platonic Academy, paving the way for Polemarchus of Nicomedia to take over. This transition marked a significant moment in the evolution of philosophical thought in ancient Greece.
events.name: Carneades retires as head of the Platonic Academy

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, Simon Thassi successfully repelled an invasion led by the Seleucid general Cendebaeus, reinforcing the Maccabean control over Judea. This victory was crucial in the ongoing struggle for Jewish autonomy against Seleucid rule.
events.name: Simon Thassi defeats an invasion by the Seleucid general Cendebaeus

events.enhanced_description: In a notable political event in Rome, the censors Appius Claudius Pulcher and Quintus Fulvius Nobilior exercised their authority to regulate public morals and conduct, reflecting the political tensions of the era. Their actions were part of a broader context of social and political reform in the Roman Republic.
events.name: Censorship of Appius Claudius Pulcher and Quintus Fulvius Nobilior

events.enhanced_description: In a controversial decision, the Roman Senate ordered the surrender of Gaius Hostilius Mancinus to the Numantians as a means to repudiate his earlier peace treaty with them. This act highlighted the complexities of Roman military and diplomatic strategies during the Numantine War.
events.name: The Romans hand Gaius Hostilius Mancinus over to the Numantians

events.enhanced_description: In 137 AD, new tax laws were implemented for trade in Palmyra, a crucial caravan city that thrived on commerce between the Mediterranean and the East. These laws facilitated the city's growth and wealth, highlighting its importance in the Roman economy.
events.name: Tax laws passed for trade in Palmyra

events.enhanced_description: While serving as quaestor in Spain, Tiberius Gracchus noted the detrimental effects of slave labor on small freehold farms. This observation would later influence his political reforms aimed at addressing social inequalities in Rome.
events.name: Tiberius Gracchus observes slave labor displacing small farms

events.enhanced_description: The Numantine War commenced with the Romans facing fierce resistance from the Numantians, culminating in the defeats of Roman generals Quintus Pompeius and M. Papilius Laenas. This conflict marked a significant chapter in the struggle between Rome and the indigenous tribes of Hispania.
events.name: Numantine War begins

events.enhanced_description: Q. Pompeius faced trial led by Q. Metellus and other officials, yet he was acquitted, reflecting the political machinations and power struggles within the Roman Republic during this period. His trial was indicative of the tensions between military leaders and the Senate.
events.name: Trial of Q. Pompeius

events.enhanced_description: In 138 AD, Emperor Hadrian appointed Antoninus Pius as his successor, with the condition that Antoninus adopt Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. This decision was pivotal in shaping the future leadership of the Roman Empire.

image.caption: Marble bust of Emperor Antoninus Pius.
image.credit: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg) — Own work
image.date_qualification: The bust is dated 138–161 AD in the image description; the 2016 date is the photograph’s original date, not the date of the depicted subject or the succession event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Hadrian makes Antoninus Pius his successor

events.enhanced_description: In 138 AD, Emperor Hadrian died from heart failure at Baiae, a luxurious resort town in Campania, Italy. He was buried in the Gardens of Domitia beside his wife, Vibia Sabina, marking the end of a significant era in Roman history.
events.name: Hadrian dies at Baiae

events.enhanced_description: In 138 AD, Antoninus Pius succeeded Hadrian as the Roman Emperor. He requested the Senate to confer divine honors upon Hadrian, reflecting the continuity of imperial reverence in Roman politics.
events.name: Antoninus Pius succeeds Hadrian as Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Theater of Philadelphia, located in modern-day Amman, Jordan, began in 138 AD. This theater became a significant cultural center in the region, showcasing the architectural prowess of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Construction begins on the Theater of Philadelphia (Amman)

events.enhanced_description: Hadrian's Villa, an expansive Roman architectural complex, was completed in 138 AD in Tivoli, Italy. This villa served as a retreat for Emperor Hadrian and is renowned for its innovative design and extensive gardens.
events.name: Hadrian's Villa is finished

events.enhanced_description: Under Emperor Antoninus Pius, the silver content of the Roman denarius decreased to 75% from 87% during Hadrian's reign in 138 AD. This change reflected the economic pressures facing the Roman Empire at the time.
events.name: The silver content of the Roman denarius falls to 75 percent

events.enhanced_description: In a pivotal moment during the Numantine War, Tautalus, a leader of the Numantians, surrendered to the Romans. This act signified a turning point in the conflict, showcasing the pressures faced by the Numantian resistance against Roman expansion.
events.name: Tautalus surrenders to the Romans

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of Valencia as a Roman colony marked an important development in the Romanization of the Iberian Peninsula. This foundation facilitated trade, agriculture, and cultural exchange, contributing to the growth of Roman influence in the region.
events.name: Valencia is founded as a Roman colony

events.enhanced_description: Attalus III ascended to the throne of Pergamon following the death of his brother Attalus II, marking a significant transition in the Attalid dynasty. His reign would later be characterized by political challenges and the eventual bequest of his kingdom to Rome.
events.name: Attalus III succeeds Attalus II as king of Pergamon

events.enhanced_description: The revolt of Galaestes represents a significant uprising against the prevailing powers of the time, reflecting the broader unrest in the region. The details of this revolt remain sparse, but it indicates the tensions present in the socio-political landscape.
events.name: Galaestes revolts

events.enhanced_description: Antiochus VII successfully expelled Diodotus Tryphon from Antioch, a significant political maneuver that reaffirmed his authority over the Seleucid Empire. This event was part of the larger power struggles within the Hellenistic world during this period.
events.name: Antiochus VII expels Diodotus Tryphon

events.enhanced_description: The sack of Beirut by Diodotus Tryphon marked a significant military action during the conflicts of the Hellenistic period, showcasing the volatility of the region. This event contributed to the shifting power dynamics among rival factions in the area.
events.name: Tryphon sacks Beirut

events.enhanced_description: Phraates II ascended to the throne of the Parthian Empire, taking control during a period marked by internal strife and external threats. His reign would be pivotal in the ongoing conflicts between Rome and Parthia.
events.name: Phraates II becomes emperor of Parthia

events.enhanced_description: Grand Empress Dowager Dou executed a significant purge of high-ranking officials, consolidating her power within the Han dynasty. This political maneuver was marked by the dismissal and arrest of key figures, reflecting the intense power struggles of the era.
events.name: Grand Empress Dowager Dou purges officials

events.enhanced_description: The composition of the Hymn to Apollo, inscribed in stone at Delphi, represents a monumental achievement in ancient music, being the earliest surviving example of notated music in the Western world. This artifact provides insight into the cultural and religious practices of ancient Greece.
events.name: Hymn to Apollo is written

events.enhanced_description: In 139 AD, the Tomb of Hadrian was completed in Rome. Emperor Antoninus Pius cremated Hadrian's body and placed his ashes alongside those of his wife, Vibia Sabina, and his adopted son, Lucius Aelius, in this monumental mausoleum.
events.name: The Tomb of Hadrian is completed

events.enhanced_description: In 139 AD, Marcus Aurelius was named Caesar and married Faustina the Younger, the daughter of Emperor Antoninus Pius. This union solidified the dynastic ties within the Roman imperial family.
events.name: Marcus Aurelius is named Caesar

events.enhanced_description: In 139 AD, Antoninus Pius and Gaius Bruttius Praesens were appointed as Roman Consuls. This event marked a significant moment in the political landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Antoninus Pius and Gaius Bruttius Praesens become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 139 AD, an earthquake struck the city of Mcurn, now known as Hösnek in Turkey. This seismic event was recorded in historical texts and is associated with the region's geological activity near Mount Ararat.
events.name: Earthquake affects the city of Mcurn

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius were appointed as Roman Consuls. This event underscored the political stability and continuity of leadership during their reign.
events.name: Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius and Marcus Aurelius Caesar become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, Emperor Antoninus Pius recognized the king of the Quadi, a Germanic tribe, as an ally of Rome. This diplomatic move was part of Rome's broader strategy to secure its borders.
events.name: Antoninus Pius recognizes the king of the Quadi

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, the export of olive oil from Hispania Baetica to Rome reached its peak. This trade was vital for the Roman economy and reflected the agricultural richness of the region.
events.name: The export of olive oil from Hispania Baetica to Rome peaks

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, King Mithridates V of the Parthian Empire died, leading to Vologases IV claiming the throne. This succession marked a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: King Mithridates V dies

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, Pope Pius I succeeded Pope Hyginus as the tenth pope of Rome according to tradition. His papacy contributed to the early development of the Christian Church.
events.name: Pope Pius I succeeds Pope Hyginus

events.enhanced_description: In 140 AD, Marcion arrived in Rome, bringing with him the Evangelikon and Apostolikon to the Christian community. His teachings would later spark significant theological debates within early Christianity.

image.caption: 11th-century Italian vellum manuscript painting depicting the Apostle John and Marcion of Sinope.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Original publication : Manuscript, Italy, 11th century Immediate source : http://corsair.themorgan.org/cgi-bin/Pwebrecon.cgi?BBID=338126
image.date_qualification: Created in the 11th century, roughly a millennium after the event dated to 140 AD; it does not document the arrival itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Marcion arrives in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Around 140 AD, the Greek astronomer Ptolemy completed his seminal work, the Almagest, in Alexandria, Egypt. This influential text laid the foundation for astronomical studies for centuries to come.
events.name: Ptolemy completes his Almagest

events.enhanced_description: In 141 AD, the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina was constructed in Rome, dedicated to Empress Faustina the Elder. This temple stands as a testament to the imperial family's legacy and architectural grandeur.
events.name: The Temple of Antoninus and Faustina is constructed

events.enhanced_description: In 141 AD, the last year of the Yonghe era of the Chinese Han Dynasty marked a significant period in Chinese history, characterized by political stability and cultural development.
events.name: Last year of Yonghe era of the Chinese Han Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 141 AD, an earthquake struck the Roman provinces of Lycia and Caria, along with the islands of Rhodes, Kos, Simi, and Serifos. The disaster triggered a severe tsunami, causing widespread devastation.
events.name: Lycia earthquake affects Roman provinces

events.enhanced_description: In 141 AD, Halley's Comet made its 6th recorded perihelion passage. This event has been noted by astronomers throughout history and is significant in the study of comets.
events.name: 6th recorded perihelion passage of Halley's Comet

events.enhanced_description: In 142 AD, Emperor Antoninus Pius ordered the construction of the Antonine Wall in Scotland. This fortification stretched 39 miles and was built to protect Roman Britain from northern tribes.
events.name: Emperor Antoninus Pius orders the construction of the Antonine Wall

events.enhanced_description: In 142 AD, the Roman Empire established the position of municipal doctors across its territories. This initiative marked a significant advancement in public health and medical care in ancient Rome.
events.name: Municipal doctors are named throughout the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 142 AD, the first year of the Hanan era of the Chinese Han Dynasty began, marking a new phase in the dynasty's history characterized by political and cultural developments.
events.name: First year of the Hanan era of the Chinese Han Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 142 AD, the Chinese Taoist alchemist Wei Boyang became the first to describe an early form of gunpowder solution. This discovery would later influence military technology in China and beyond.
events.name: Wei Boyang describes early gunpowder solution

events.enhanced_description: In 142 AD, Marcion proclaimed that the Old Testament was incompatible with Christianity, a controversial stance that would lead to significant theological debates within the early Church.
events.name: Marcion proclaims Old Testament incompatibility with Christianity

events.enhanced_description: Antoninus Pius, a prominent Roman Emperor, served as Consul, a significant political office in the Roman Republic and Empire, which allowed him to exert influence over the governance of Rome.
events.name: Antoninus Pius serves as Roman Consul

events.enhanced_description: The Brigantes, a powerful tribe in Roman Britain, revolted against Roman rule but were suppressed by the Roman governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus, demonstrating the ongoing tensions between the Roman Empire and indigenous tribes.

locations.name: York, North Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom

events.name: A revolt of the Brigantes tribe in Britannia is suppressed by Quintus Lollius Urbicus

events.enhanced_description: Antyllus, a Roman physician, is credited with performing the first arteriotomy, a groundbreaking surgical procedure that laid the foundation for future advancements in medical practices.
events.name: The Roman doctor Antyllus performs the first arteriotomy

events.enhanced_description: The Celtiberian War, a conflict between the Roman Republic and the Celtiberian tribes, concluded with a decisive victory for the Romans under the command of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus. This victory solidified Roman control over the region and marked a significant moment in the expansion of Roman influence in Hispania.
events.name: The Celtiberian War ends when Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus crushes the rebels

events.enhanced_description: Lucius Hedius Rufus Lollianus Avitus and Titus Statilius Maximus were appointed as Roman Consuls, a prestigious position that allowed them to influence the political landscape of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Lucius Hedius Rufus Lollianus Avitus and Titus Statilius Maximus become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: The Roman Empire initiated military campaigns in Mauretania, a region in North Africa, to expand its territory and consolidate control over the local tribes.
events.name: The Roman campaigns in Mauretania begin

events.enhanced_description: The Han dynasty officially changed the era name from Hanan to Jiankang, marking a new period in its history and reflecting the political and cultural shifts of the time.
events.name: Change of era name from Hanan to Jiankang era of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The transition of power from Emperor Han Shundi to Emperor Han Chongdi marked a significant change in leadership within the Han dynasty, influencing the political landscape of China.
events.name: Change of emperor from Han Shundi to Han Chongdi of the Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Huvishka ascended to the throne of the Kushan Empire, overseeing a period of prosperity and cultural exchange that significantly impacted the regions of Central and South Asia.

locations.name: Kushan Empire, modern-day Afghanistan and northern India

events.name: Reign of Huvishka, emperor of the Kushan Empire

events.enhanced_description: The transition of the Patriarchate from Polycarpus II to Athendodorus marked a significant change in the leadership of the Christian community in Constantinople, influencing religious practices and politics.
events.name: Change of Patriarch of Constantinople from Polycarpus II to Athendodorus

events.enhanced_description: Marcion of Sinope was excommunicated from the Christian church, leading to the formation of Marcionism, a sect that emphasized a distinct interpretation of Christian doctrine and the nature of God.
events.name: Marcion of Sinope is excommunicated; a sect, Marcionism, grows out of his beliefs

events.enhanced_description: The Aqua Marcia, one of the longest aqueducts in ancient Rome, was initiated by Quintus Marcius Rex, significantly improving the water supply to the city. This engineering marvel is notable for its length and the quality of its water, which was considered among the best available in Rome.
events.name: Quintus Marcius Rex starts construction of the Aqua Marcia aqueduct in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Parthian Empire expanded its territory by conquering Babylonia, a region rich in history and culture. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the Near East, as the Parthians established their influence over former territories of the Seleucid Empire.
events.name: Parthians take Babylonia

events.enhanced_description: Antoninus Pius and his adopted son Marcus Aurelius were appointed as Roman Consuls, a role that allowed them to jointly oversee the administration of the Roman Empire during a time of relative peace.
events.name: Antoninus Augustus Pius and Marcus Aurelius Caesar become Roman Consuls

events.enhanced_description: The marriage of Marcus Aurelius to Faustina the Younger, daughter of Antoninus Pius, strengthened political alliances and established a lineage that would influence the future of the Roman Empire.
events.name: Marcus Aurelius marries Faustina the Younger, the daughter of Antoninus Pius

events.enhanced_description: Arrian, a notable historian and philosopher, was appointed as archon in Athens, a position that allowed him to influence the civic and cultural life of the city.
events.name: Arrian becomes archon in Athens

events.enhanced_description: The succession from Emperor Han Chongdi to Emperor Han Zhidi marked a pivotal moment in the Han dynasty, influencing the political dynamics and governance of China.
events.name: Change of emperor from Han Chongdi to Han Zhidi of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Ptolemy VII ascended to the throne of Egypt, albeit briefly, before being assassinated by his brother Ptolemy VIII. This power struggle exemplified the tumultuous nature of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the intense rivalries within it.
events.name: Ptolemy VII becomes king of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Hipparchus, a prominent Greek astronomer, made significant contributions to the understanding of the tropical year, establishing its length with remarkable precision for his time. His work laid the foundation for future astronomical studies and calendar systems.
events.name: Hipparchus determines the length of the tropical year

events.enhanced_description: Faustina the Younger was bestowed the title of Augusta, officially recognizing her as Roman Empress and solidifying her role in the imperial family.
events.name: Faustina the Younger is given the title Augusta, and becomes Roman Empress

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Aurelius was granted the imperium proconsular, a significant military and administrative authority, which empowered him to govern and lead the Roman Empire effectively.
events.name: Marcus Aurelius receives the imperium proconsular

events.enhanced_description: The Han dynasty transitioned from the Yongxi era to the Benchu era, marking a new phase in its governance and reflecting the changing political landscape of the time.
events.name: Change of era name from Yongxi to Benchu era of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The ascension of Han Huandi to the throne marked a significant transition in the Han dynasty, influencing the future direction of Chinese governance and policy.
events.name: Han Huandi succeeds Han Zhidi as emperor of the Chinese Han dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Chadae ascended to power as the ruler of Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, influencing the region's political landscape and interactions with neighboring states.

locations.name: Goguryeo, modern-day North Korea and northeastern China

events.name: Chadae becomes ruler of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo

events.enhanced_description: The Roman Republic decisively destroyed both Carthage and Corinth, marking the end of significant resistance in the Mediterranean. These events not only signified the fall of two powerful city-states but also established Rome's dominance in the region, leading to a new era of Roman control.
events.name: Roman armies destroy Carthage and Corinth

events.enhanced_description: The Achaean War concluded with the Roman conquest of the Achaean League, leading to the establishment of southern Greece as a Roman province. This event marked a significant expansion of Roman territory and influence in the Greek world.
events.name: Achaean War: The Romans conquer the Achaean League

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Scarpheia saw the Roman forces, led by Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus, achieve victory over the Achaean League led by Critolaus. This battle was crucial in the Romans' campaign to subdue the Achaean League and assert their dominance in Greece.
events.name: Battle of Scarpheia

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, King Antigonus II of Macedonia defeated the Spartans and killed King Areus I near Corinth, marking a pivotal moment in the struggle for control in southern Greece. Following this victory, Antigonus besieged Athens, further consolidating Macedonian power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Corinth

events.enhanced_description: Hipparchus made significant advancements in astronomy by determining the equinoctial point, contributing to the understanding of celestial movements. His work was foundational for future astronomers and played a crucial role in the development of the science of astronomy.
events.name: Hipparchus determines the equinoctial point

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 146 BC, Carthage fell to the Roman general Scipio Aemilianus, culminating in the complete destruction of the city. This event marked the end of the Third Punic War and solidified Rome's status as the preeminent power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Carthage falls to Roman forces under Scipio Aemilianus

events.enhanced_description: Marcus Aurelius was granted imperial powers by Emperor Antoninus Pius, positioning him as a key figure in the governance of the Roman Empire and setting the stage for his future reign.
events.name: Marcus Aurelius receives imperial powers, from Emperor Antoninus Pius

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Antoninus Pius hosted grand festivals to commemorate the 900th anniversary of Rome's founding, celebrating the city's rich history and cultural heritage.
events.name: Festivals to celebrate the 900th anniversary of the founding of Rome begin

events.enhanced_description: King Vologases III of the Parthian Empire passed away after a lengthy reign of 42 years, during which he successfully navigated political challenges and maintained stability in the region.
events.name: King Vologases III dies after a 42-year reign

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, King Vologases IV ascended to the throne and successfully united the Parthian Empire, strengthening its political structure and influence in the region.
events.name: King Vologases IV unites the Parthian Empire under his rule

events.enhanced_description: The first year of the Jianhe era in the Han Dynasty marked a new chapter in Chinese history, reflecting the political and cultural developments of the time.
events.name: First year of Jianhe of the Chinese Han Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The Corlea Trackway, an ancient wooden trackway in Ireland, was completed, showcasing the engineering skills of the time. This significant archaeological site provides insight into the early use of infrastructure in prehistoric Ireland.
events.name: Corlea Trackway completed

events.enhanced_description: Scipio Aemilianus assumed command of the Siege of Carthage, leading Roman forces in the final assault against the city. His leadership was pivotal in the eventual destruction of Carthage, marking a significant moment in Roman military history.
events.name: Scipio Aemilianus takes command of the Siege of Carthage

events.enhanced_description: In Lusitania, the Celtic king Viriathus emerged as a leader of resistance against Roman expansion, uniting various tribes in a struggle for independence. His leadership marked a significant chapter in the history of Roman-Lusitanian conflicts and showcased the fierce resistance of indigenous peoples.
events.name: Viriathus rallies Lusitanian resistance to Rome

events.enhanced_description: Demetrius II of Syria returned to his kingdom after a period of exile, marking a significant moment in the political landscape of the Seleucid Empire. His return aimed to restore his rule and stabilize the region amidst ongoing conflicts and rivalries.
events.name: Demetrius II of Syria returns to Syria

events.enhanced_description: Jonathan Maccabaeus, a leader of the Maccabean Revolt, successfully captured the coastal city of Joppa, which was crucial for securing trade routes and military supplies. This victory further solidified the Maccabean control over Judea and demonstrated their military prowess against Hellenistic forces.
events.name: Jonathan Maccabaeus conquers Joppa

events.enhanced_description: In 147 BC, Macedonia was formally annexed into the Roman Empire, marking the end of its status as an independent kingdom. This incorporation was part of Rome's broader strategy to consolidate power in the eastern Mediterranean and manage its expanding territories.
events.name: Macedonia becomes a part of the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: To celebrate the 900th anniversary of Rome, Emperor Antoninus Pius organized grand games that showcased the empire's wealth and cultural achievements, fostering a sense of unity among its citizens.
events.name: Emperor Antoninus Pius hosts a series of grand games

events.enhanced_description: An Shigao, a prominent Buddhist monk, arrives in Luoyang, China, marking a significant moment in the spread of Buddhism in the region. His teachings and translations would greatly influence Chinese Buddhism and its integration into Chinese culture.
events.name: An Shigao arrives in China

events.enhanced_description: Euzois takes over the position of Patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Athendodorus. This transition is significant in the context of the early Christian church's influence in the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Euzois succeeds Athendodorus, as Patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: The Corlea Trackway, an ancient wooden road, was constructed in County Longford, Ireland, showcasing the engineering capabilities of the Iron Age people in the region. This significant archaeological site provides insights into the transportation and trade practices of early Irish societies.
events.name: Corlea Trackway built in County Longford

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pydna was a decisive confrontation in which Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus defeated Andriscus, the last king of Macedon. This victory led to the reorganization of Macedon as a Roman province, significantly altering the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Battle of Pydna

events.enhanced_description: The Via Postumia was constructed to connect the cities of Aquileia and Genua, facilitating trade and military movement across northern Italy. This road became a vital artery for the Roman Empire, enhancing economic integration and administrative control in the region.
events.name: Construction of the Via Postumia

events.enhanced_description: Scipio Aemilianus divided the kingdom of Numidia among the three sons of Masinissa, following the latter's death. This political maneuvering was aimed at stabilizing the region and ensuring Roman influence over North Africa.
events.name: Division of Numidia by Scipio Aemilianus

events.enhanced_description: The Third Punic War commenced as Roman forces landed in Africa, initiating hostilities against Carthage. This conflict would culminate in the complete destruction of Carthage and the further expansion of Roman power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: The Third Punic War begins

events.enhanced_description: Servius Sulpicius Galba faced prosecution for corruption during his tenure in Hispania, but managed to evade conviction by leveraging public sympathy through a display of his distressed family. This incident highlighted the complexities of Roman legal and political systems.
events.name: Servius Sulpicius Galba's corruption trial

events.enhanced_description: The passage of the lex Calpurnia de repetundis by Lucius Calpurnius Piso established the first permanent criminal court in Rome, marking a significant development in the Roman legal system. This legislation aimed to curb corruption among provincial governors and enhance accountability.
events.name: Lex Calpurnia de repetundis

events.enhanced_description: The Lusitanian War reignited under the leadership of Viriathus, as tensions escalated between Roman forces and the indigenous tribes of Hispania. This conflict exemplified the ongoing resistance against Roman expansion and the struggle for autonomy among the local populations.
events.name: Renewal of the Lusitanian War

events.enhanced_description: Andriscus, claiming to be the rightful heir to the Macedonian throne, ascended to power amidst a backdrop of political instability. His reign marked the last flicker of independence for Macedon before its eventual annexation by Rome.
events.name: Andriscus ascends to the throne of Macedon

events.enhanced_description: With the support of Roman forces, Nicomedes II successfully overthrew his father, Prusias II, to become king of Bithynia. This power shift exemplified the influence of Roman politics in the region and the strategic alliances formed during this period.
events.name: Nicomedes II overthrows Prusias II

events.enhanced_description: The Roman town of Forum Hadriani, located in present-day Voorburg, is granted the title of Municipium Aelium Cananefatium, allowing it to organize markets and gain greater autonomy. This reflects the Roman Empire's administrative practices and the integration of local communities.
events.name: The Roman town Forum Hadriani receives the title of Municipium Aelium Cananefatium
